Within families affected, the disease may present at different ages. It can affect different parts of the body and progress at different rates. This is because changes in the C9orf7 gene, which can cause familial MND, can also cause FTD. 2 Some people who don’t have a family history of MND (sporadic MND) can still have a change in the genes that cause MND. 3 ##### What is a gene change? DNA gives instructions to every cell in the body to help it grow and work. A gene change is an error in the genetic DNA code that causes a gene to work abnormally. It is sometimes called a ‘gene mutation’ or ‘gene fault’. A gene change can be passed on from a parent to a child. If a person has an MND-related gene change, each child has a 50 percentage chance of inheriting it. 4 If the gene change is present in your family, you have a higher risk of being diagnosed with MND. The most common MND-related genes are: - C9ORF72 - SOD1 - FUS - TDP-43 ## Genetic testing and counselling Deciding whether to have genetic testing is a personal decision. Some people will want to find out if they carry a MND-related gene change, while others will not. Genetic testing is done by collecting DNA, typically from a small blood sample or cheek swab. Reasons to consider genetic testing include: 5 - to understand if there is a genetic cause to your disease (if you have MND) - to clarify whether or not you are at risk of developing MND (if a MND-related gene change has been found in your family) - to access potential treatments that are specific

Your GP can refer you to a genetic counselling service where you can speak to someone who will help you to better understand the process. Predictive testing typically involves having one or more appointments with a genetic counsellor and/or a geneticist (a doctor with specialised training). Predictive genetic testing is usually only accessible when there is a known MND-related gene change in the family. If there is a history of MND in your family, but there isn’t a known gene change, you may still be able to access genetic counselling to further discuss your risk of MND. ## What do genetic counsellors do? Genetic counsellors are not psychologists; they are trained in medical genetics and counselling. Their role is to give information, support and guidance throughout the genetic testing process. Genetic counsellors can assist with the following: - give information about genetic testing and how it works - explore your family history and look at your family tree - explore the benefits and limitations of genetic testing - explain your options - help you to explore what the results might mean for you and others - help you make an informed decision about whether to proceed with testing - talk through the results with you and help you adjust to the news - support you in communicating results to family members. If you have been referred to a genetic counselling service to discuss your family history of MND, it’s a good idea to gather the following to share with your genetic counsellor: - family history information of MND, dementia, Parkinson’s or similar conditions - documents confirming a clinical diagnosis in a relative - family letter from a genetic service or any previous genetic testing reports from other family members. ## What are my options if I am planning to start a family? If you have a family history of MND and are planning to start a family, you may be concerned about passing on an MND-related gene change. Genetic counsellors can give information and support and discuss reproductive options. You can also talk to your GP or a psychologist. If you know which gene change is causing MND in your family, and would like to consider testing, there are two main options: Pre-implantation genetic testing (PGT-M) PGT-M is a specialised type of in vitro fertilisation (IVF). In PGT-M, embryos are created outside the body and tested for the presence/absence of the MND gene change. Only unaffected embryos are considered suitable to be placed into the womb. 6 IVF clinics offering PGT-M can provide further information on PGT-M. They can also provide information on the associated costs and the Medicare rebates available. Prenatal diagnosis (PND) Prenatal diagnosis (PND) testing is done during pregnancy. The test checks to see whether the baby also has the gene change. PND testing typically includes: - Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) - Amniocentesis. 7 PND testing takes place in the first or second trimester. For more information visit The Centre for Genetics Education or speak to a genetic counselling service. Additional options include: Having children without genetic testing This means accepting the chance that the genetic condition may be passed on to your child. Having children using donor eggs or sperm This involves having in vitro fertilisation (IVF) using eggs or sperm from a donor, rather than from the parent at risk of MND. This ensures you avoid passing on the genetic condition. ##### I don’t want to know if I carry my family’s

Can I still access testing to inform family planning? If you don’t want to know if you have inherited the gene change, exclusion testing may be an option. Exclusion testing can be done using PGT-M and PND to identify if a baby/embryo is at risk, without revealing the parent’s genetic status. ## Genetic testing – some challenges ##### Accessing genetic testing Not everyone can access testing, even if they would like to get tested. It can be especially difficult in cases where there isn’t already a known gene change within a family, and you don’t have a confirmed diagnosis of MND, even if there is MND within the family. Once you have had the test, it may take up to 6 months to get your results. You will be contacted once the result is available. Check with your doctor if you have not received your results within 6 months. 8 ##### Testing costs Some genetic services may give subsidised or free testing for MND-related genes. This only applies if you have a diagnosis of MND or if someone in your family carries a known gene change. Some services may be expensive. Cost depends on the following: - the type of testing conducted (diagnostic or predictive) - the type of genetic services you access (public versus private). Until then, there are rules in place that stop insurers using your genetic test results to refuse you basic life insurance or charge you more for it. This means you do not need to disclose your test results as part of a life insurance application if applying for cover below a specific threshold (typically a minimal level of cover). For more information about genetic testing and insurance, visit The Centre for Genetics Education or speak to a financial advisor. ## More information ###### Animations and videos - Genetics and MND Animation explaining how an MND gene can run in families, genetic testing and more. - Inherited MND – healthtalk.org Series of interviews with people living with familial MND (UK). ###### Support and

text: mutation. The remaining 90% of people are said to have ‘sporadic’ MND. Most people with MND have the sporadic form. It is not a genetic form of the condition and it will not be passed on in families. The genetic form of MND can be passed on in future generations and affect multiple family members over time. People who have this form of MND have inherited a genetic mutation from one of their parents. If a person has an MND-related genetic mutation each of their children has a 50/50 chance of inheriting the MND-related genetic mutation. ## Genetic testing Clinical genetic testing is a personal decision and complex process. The first stage of this process is a genetic counselling session and initial consultation. Part of the counselling process involves advising potential outcomes, costs involved, and ramifications of testing. If you would like to access genetic testing then you will need a referral from your GP that details that you require genetic testing as you have a family history of MND.

This ban will come into effect on 8 October 2026. The HGSA published a Position Statement Genetic Testing and Personal Insurance Products in Australia . From July 2019 there has been a moratorium in regard to requirements of disclosure of genetic test results in life insurance product applications at a level below $500,000 for death and total and permanent disability, $200,000 for trauma, $4,000 a month for income protection. text: NMDs present antenatally or in early infancy, and are associated with significant disability or life-threatening complications. While historically, treatment options for NMDs were poor, new developments offer curative interventions or improvements in the decrease of morbidity and mortality. NMDs tend to be genetic in origin, and can be inherited as autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked, or mitochondrial traits. However, de novo pathogenic variants are relatively common. Therefore, novel treatments for NMDs are guided by the underlying molecular pathology and establishment of a definitive genetic diagnosis. NMDs can be roughly allocated into four categories: muscle disorders (such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy); motor neuron disorders (including spinal muscular atrophy); neuropathies (such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease); and neuromuscular junction disorders. ## Application documents ### Application form Download 1585%20Redacted%20Application%20Form.pdf as PDF - 2 MB Download 1585%20Redacted%20Application%20Form.docx as Word - 442 KB ### Consultation survey Download 1585%20Consultation%20Survey.pdf as PDF - 487 KB Download 1585%20Consultation%20Survey.docx as Word - 71 KB ### PICO confirmation Download 1585%20Ratified%20PICO.pdf as PDF - 2 MB Download 1585%20Ratified%20PICO.docx as Word - 317 KB

Genetics, family risk and genetic testing record: Familial MND and inherited risk Category: familial_mnd Publisher: MND Australia URL: https://www.mndaustralia.org.au/mnd-connect/information-resources/familial-mnd-and-genetic-testing Description: Australian MND-specific information on familial or inherited MND, common gene changes, family risk, sporadic MND and why genetic factors do not always mean a person will develop MND. Care team notes: Use careful wording: a gene change can increase risk, but it does not guarantee MND. Encourage discussion with neurologist, MND clinic or genetic counselling service.

source_title: Diagnostic genetic testing after MND diagnosis
text: Genetics, family risk and genetic testing record: Diagnostic genetic testing after MND diagnosis Category: diagnostic_genetic_testing Publisher: MND Australia URL: https://www.mndaustralia.org.au/mnd-connect/information-resources/familial-mnd-and-genetic-testing Description: Explains diagnostic genetic testing for people already diagnosed with MND, including possible reasons to test, gene-targeted treatment/trial relevance and storage of DNA samples where appropriate. Care team notes: Do not recommend a specific test. Suggest asking the treating neurologist what test is appropriate, how long results may take, what it may cost and whether counselling is available.

source_title: Predictive genetic testing for family members
text: Genetics, family risk and genetic testing record: Predictive genetic testing for family members Category: predictive_testing Publisher: MND Australia / MND NSW URL: https://www.mndnsw.org.au/about-mnd/what-is-mnd/654-does-mnd-have-a-genetic-connection.html Description: Information for relatives asking whether MND runs in the family, including predictive testing, GP referral, genetic counselling and known family gene-change requirements. Care team notes: Flag that predictive testing is a personal decision with emotional and family implications. Recommend genetic counselling before testing.

source_title: Genetic counselling before and after testing
publisher: MND Australia / Centre for Genetics Education
text: Genetics, family risk and genetic testing record: Genetic counselling before and after testing Category: genetic_counselling Publisher: MND Australia / Centre for Genetics Education URL: https://www.mndaustralia.org.au/mnd-connect/information-resources/familial-mnd-and-genetic-testing Description: Explains what genetic counsellors do, how counselling supports decision-making, and why counselling matters for diagnostic and predictive MND genetic testing. Care team notes: For patient-facing answers, frame counselling as support for choice and understanding, not as pressure to test.

Genetics, family risk and genetic testing record: Family planning and reproductive options Category: family_planning Publisher: MND Australia URL: https://www.mndaustralia.org.au/mnd-connect/information-resources/familial-mnd-and-genetic-testing Description: Australian MND-specific information on options for people planning a family where an MND-related gene change is known, including genetic counselling and pre-implantation/prenatal discussion pathways. Care team notes: Keep answers neutral and values-sensitive. Refer to genetic counsellor/fertility specialist for medical, ethical and cost details.

source_title: Genetic testing and life insurance in Australia
publisher: Centre for Genetics Education / Human Genetics Society of Australasia / Federal Register of Legislation
text: Genetics, family risk and genetic testing record: Genetic testing and life insurance in Australia Category: insurance_and_genetic_discrimination Publisher: Centre for Genetics Education / Human Genetics Society of Australasia / Federal Register of Legislation URL: https://www.genetics.edu.au/SitePages/Life-insurance-products-and-genetic-testing-in-Australia.aspx Description: Current Australian information on genetic testing and life insurance, including the 8 October 2026 commencement of new protections and the interim moratorium context. Care team notes: This is high-stakes financial/legal information. Encourage checking current guidance and speaking with a genetic counsellor or financial/legal adviser before applying for insurance or testing.

source_title: Australian assessment of genetic testing for familial neuromuscular disorders
text: Genetics, family risk and genetic testing record: Australian assessment of genetic testing for familial neuromuscular disorders Category: australian_testing_access_policy Publisher: Medical Services Advisory Committee URL: https://www.msac.gov.au/applications/1585 Description: Australian MSAC application/outcome information for genetic testing in early-onset or familial neuromuscular disorders, useful for explaining Australian public funding/policy context. Care team notes: Do not translate MSAC outcome into guaranteed patient eligibility. Use it as policy context and direct people to their neurologist/genetics service for individual access.

source_title: Gene-targeted treatment and clinical trial context
text: Genetics, family risk and genetic testing record: Gene-targeted treatment and clinical trial context Category: gene_targeted_treatment Publisher: MND Australia / MND Association UK URL: https://www.mndaustralia.org.au/mnd-connect/information-resources/familial-mnd-and-genetic-testing Description: Explains why genetic testing may matter for gene-targeted treatment or trial eligibility, while preserving that non-Australian treatment or regulatory information must not be applied to Australia unless confirmed by Australian sources. Care team notes: When answering about tofersen/SOD1 or trials, cross-reference Topic 14 treatments and Topic 17 clinical trials. State when a supporting source is UK or otherwise non-Australian.

Genetics, family risk and genetic testing record: Non-Australian inherited MND support material Category: non_australian_context Publisher: MND Association UK URL: https://www.mndassociation.org/about-mnd/mnd-explained/inherited-mnd Description: UK/US explanatory material on inherited MND and genetic testing experiences, retained only as labelled non-Australian context where Australian sources do not provide enough detail. Care team notes: Use after Australian sources. Always label as UK/US context and avoid applying non-Australian service, funding or insurance rules to Australian users.
